newsitem.title: MEXICO: New leader of Mexico's PRI aims to rescue party.
newsitem.headline: New leader of Mexico's PRI aims to rescue party.

text.p: Humberto Roque Villanueva, who was due to be elected on Sunday as the new president of Mexico's long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), said his mandate will be to rescue the party from the crisis that threatens to topple its 67-year grip on power.

"We have enthusiasm (in the party), we have warmth and I say that not only is there salvation but also that we are not lost," newspapers quoted Roque as saying in an impromptu press conference late on Saturday.

"We have to get it across to the whole country that not only are we alive ... but that we are prepared to face the risks of elections," he added, after officially registering his candidacy for the party presidency.
The PRI has suffered a series of problems lately, including humiliating state and town hall election defeats, embarassing defections of members to the opposition and party infighting.

Santiago Onate Labourde, who had been PRI president for 16 months, stepped down on Friday. In his resignation letter, he said the time had come for a renewed leadership. Critics say he became a scapegoat for the PRI's failings.
Roque, a close ally of President Ernesto Zedillo, is the sole candidate for the PRI leadership post and was expected to be elected by the party's National Executive Committee on Sunday.
His leadership role and style will be pivotal for the PRI in the run-up to crucial mid-term elections next summer, where the challenge for the party will be to hang on to its congressional majority.
The PRI has governed Mexico, holding the presidency and parliamentary majorities, for almost seven decades.
Interior Minister Emilio Chuayffet Chemor admitted on Friday the PRI needed to change to hang onto power. "The PRI has to change even the way it walks," he told reporters.
That challenge has fallen squarely on the shoulders of Roque, who was until this week was the powerful 53-year-old PRI leader of the lower house of congress.
A self-confessed Zedillista (follower of the president) and "political animal," Roque is known as a skilful negotiator, even with opposition congressmen.
"For me, the most important, the most prestigious asset that PRI counts on is called Ernesto Zedillo," Roque said, according to newspaper reports.
His academic background is in economics, making him more akin to Zedillo's technocrat-filled Cabinet than Onate, who was much more a traditional career politician.

Roque cemented his friendship with Zedillo when the two worked closely together in the administration of ex-president Carlos Salinas. Roque was chairman of congress's Planning and Budget Committee when Zedillo was deputy minister of that branch of the Finance Ministry.

But Roque was heavily criticised recently for an uncouth gesture when he failed to control his delight after he won a tense vote to increase taxes. PRI congressmen had threatened to oppose the bill, but Roque dissauded them from toppling the presidential initiative.
Opposition parties have decried the leadership change, saying it was just window-dressing to cover up the PRI's internal crisis.

"They (the PRI members) want to put fresh paint on a building that is falling down, but they have to realise they cannot continue monopolising power," Armando Quintero, a leader of the leftist Democratic Revolution Party (PRD) told reporters.
